records.question: When must U.S. Treasury trades be centrally cleared, and which clearinghouses can do it?
records.answer: Under the SEC rule adopted December 13, 2023, eligible secondary-market Treasury cash trades must be centrally cleared by December 31, 2026, and repo by June 30, 2027; the SEC said in February 2025 it does not intend further extensions. Three clearinghouses are registered to do it: FICC (DTCC's subsidiary, the incumbent), CME Securities Clearing (registered December 1, 2025; its launch moved from Q2 to 'later in 2026') and ICE Clear Credit (its Treasury business approved January 30, 2026). The mandate does not apply to the Fed's own operations; clearing those is still only a proposal.

records.question: Which Fed technology projects are live, and which are only proposed?
records.answer: Of 17 Fed technology projects the library tracks, 9 are live (FedNow and its add-ons, the Reserve Banks' shared AI platform, Richmond's national IT, the New York repo platform, Philadelphia's collateral systems, Treasury central clearing and DTC's tokenized entitlements), 1 is an authorized but limited account (Kraken), 2 are scheduled (the 2027 FedNow discount and longer Fedwire hours in 2028 or 2029), 2 are proposals (the Payment Account and the Fed's stablecoin rules) and 3 are research only.

records.question: Which Reserve Bank runs which national payment and Treasury service?
records.answer: The Fed's national services are spread across the twelve Reserve Banks, each a separate legal corporation. Boston runs FedNow; New York runs Fedwire Funds, Fedwire Securities and the National Settlement Service and carries out the Fed's open-market operations; Atlanta runs check and FedACH; Chicago runs FedLine access; Cleveland builds Treasury's Pay.gov; Minneapolis supports TreasuryDirect; Richmond hosts the System's national IT; Kansas City decides account requests.

records.question: Which banks have used Swift's blockchain ledger, and for what?
records.answer: Swift lists 17 banks for its blockchain ledger. 8 of them appear in 6 transactions the banks themselves published, which they call live pilots. Swift says most of the 17 have transacted, so some have not been named.

records.question: What have courts decided about who gets a Fed account?
records.answer: So far the courts side with the Fed. Two appeals courts (the Tenth Circuit for Custodia in 2025 and the Second Circuit for Banco San Juan in 2026) held that being eligible for a Fed account does not entitle a bank to one. Custodia has asked the Supreme Court to take the case, and the Fed opposed review on October 13, 2026.

records.question: Did the ban on 'reputation risk' debanking become law, and at which agencies?
records.answer: It became agency regulation, not a law passed by Congress: the OCC and FDIC adopted a final rule (April 10, 2026); the NCUA adopted a final rule (June 25, 2026); the Federal Reserve Board has only proposed one (February 26, 2026). The NCUA's rule says it implements Executive Order 14331 (signed August 7, 2025 · published August 12, 2025).

records.question: Who really owns your loan?
records.answer: Often not the bank or brand you see. In Affirm's program agreements filed with the SEC (November 2020), Cross River Bank is the named lender, Affirm buys most of the loans, owns the customer information and services them, and Upstart processes applications and keeps the register of who owns the note. On the library's July 11, 2026 reading, the Affirm Card is issued by Evolve or Stride, not Cross River, and Upstart's note permits sale without borrower consent and discloses the owner only on written request.

records.question: What changes in your card or bank contract when your bank is sold?
records.answer: The library follows 6 bank sales and card-program moves since April 1, 2025 (Ally / Merrick, Capital One / Discover, Goldman, Fifth Third, Bilt / Column, PNC). In each, the brand, card number or app stays while the legal bank behind it changes, and the customer's new terms arrive on a separate, later clock; 2 conversions (Fifth Third, Goldman) have no customer contract published yet.

records.question: How are big banks limiting group lawsuits in their customer contracts?
records.answer: Through their customer agreements: across 12 dated records from November 2018 to June 4, 2026, the library documents 8 banks and card issuers (Bank of America, Bread / Comenity, Chase, Citi, Cross River, PNC, Synchrony, Truist) using individual arbitration, waivers of class and group claims, and short mailed opt-out windows, and 3 records add special rules for mass filings. Each card links the contract or notice it comes from.

records.question: Has the federal government really stopped sending paper checks?
records.answer: Mostly, not entirely. Executive Order 14247 (signed March 25, 2025 · published March 28, 2025) ordered an end to paper checks for federal payments, and a customs notice of July 8, 2026 says the government no longer sends them; but the Treasury's own April 29, 2026 proposal still sets out when agencies may send one, and the PBGC was moving its remaining paper-check recipients on June 24, 2026. In FY2026 Treasury screened >1.1 billion payment requests (about $3.7 trillion) before the money went out.
